title: Use Selective Honesty and Generosity to Disarm Your Victim
summary: Selective honesty and generosity disarm people by lowering their guard and creating a positive, trusting impression. Strategic acts of truthfulness or calculated gifts distract victims from underlying ulterior motives, making them vulnerable to deception.
example: A con artist earned a gangster's trust and a $5,000 reward by returning $50,000 intact while politely admitting failure to double it.
The Romans gifted a giant wooden horse to Troy as a false sign of surrender, concealing soldiers inside to conquer the city.
King Wu of China gained the trust of Hu by marrying his daughter to Hu's ruler and executing or reprimanding a minister who suggested attacking them, before launching a surprise invasion.
Gordon built trust with Gould using an expert handwriting demonstration before secretly selling off his railway shares for profit.
A Roman general won over the Faliscans without a prolonged siege by returning their children along with their treacherous teacher stripped and whipped.
reversal: If you already have a history or reputation of deceit, selective honesty or generosity will fail to deceive.
When your deceit is known, acting as a dishonest person can build trust because people trust a dishonest person to act dishonestly, such as Lustig posing as a corrupt official expecting a bribe.
Embracing total unpredictability or presenting blatant contradictions can serve as an alternative smokescreen when your dishonest reputation precedes you.
